message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | Your Rights (Texas) | What It Means for You | |------|---------------------|-----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs or cleaning. If the landlord keeps part of the deposit, they must provide a written itemized statement. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Must comply with all applicable building, health, and safety codes. | If something is broken (e.g., a leaky roof, broken heater), you can notify the landlord in writing and give them a reasonable time to fix it. | | **Repair & Maintenance** | • Landlord must repair major problems that affect habitability.
• If the landlord fails to repair, you may:
 1. **Withhold rent** (after giving written notice and a 10‑day cure period).
 2. **Repair and deduct** (pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but only if the repair is less than $500).
 3. **Terminate the lease** (if the problem is serious and not fixed). | Keep records of all communications and receipts for any repairs you pay for. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter your unit without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) and a legitimate reason (e.g., repairs, inspections).
• Entry is prohibited during **nighttime** unless you consent. | If a landlord enters without notice or for an improper reason, you can ask them to stop and may pursue legal action. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy and cannot harass or threaten you. | Document any harassment or threats. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• The lease can’t contain illegal or unconscionable terms. | Review your lease carefully; if you suspect a clause is illegal, seek advice. | | **Rent Increases** | • For most residential leases, the landlord can increase rent only at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• No “no‑increase” clauses are enforceable. | Keep track of rent changes and ensure the landlord follows the required notice period. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | If you believe you’ve been discriminated against, you can file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Eviction** | • Landlord must follow the legal eviction process (notice, court filing, judgment).
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, lease violation, or owner’s intent to occupy. | If you receive an eviction notice, you have the right to respond in court. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for:
 • Unpaid rent
 • Damage beyond normal wear and tear
 • Cleaning costs if the unit is not left in a reasonable condition | Landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions. | | **Right to Repair** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may **repair and deduct** (up to $500) or **terminate the lease**. | Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases, either party must give **30 days’ written notice** to terminate. | Ensure any notice you give is in writing and dated. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Landlord may prohibit subletting, but if allowed, you must follow the lease terms. | Obtain written permission if you plan to sublet. | ### Practical Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, texts, and a written log of any maintenance requests and responses. 2. **Know Your Lease** – Read it thoroughly; if a clause seems unfair or illegal, discuss it with the landlord or seek legal counsel. 3. **Use Written Notices** – When reporting problems or giving notice, use written communication (email or certified mail) so you have proof. 4. **Know the Timeline** – For repairs, the landlord typically has 10 days to fix major issues after you notify them. For rent increases, they must give 30 days’ notice. 5. **Seek Help if Needed** – If you face eviction, discrimination, or a landlord who refuses to comply with Texas law, you can contact: - Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) - Texas Commission on Human Rights - Local tenant‑rights groups or legal aid organizations --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may alter how the law applies. If you have a particular issue or need legal guidance, consider consulting a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
